clue.text: Dares division before this peace in Africa

definitions.text: Dares division before this peace in Africa

parts.words: Dares division before this peace in Africa
parts.note: split the word Dares into Dar es, put the Arabic greeting meaning peace after it, and you have the old capital of Tanzania, an African city

explanation.surface: A treaty in Africa is preceded by a split over who dares what.
explanation.walkthrough: Dar es Salaam, the Tanzanian port, means 'haven of peace'; 'Dares division' asks you to break Dares into Dar es, and the word that follows in the city's name is the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: The Arabic greeting is literally the word for peace, used as a respectful salutation.

parts.note: 'Penchant' is split as 'pen chant': a bird's chant at the end, or a final piece of written work

explanation.surface: Someone's fondness for completing jobs.
explanation.walkthrough: The legendary swan sings only as it dies, so its song is a final performance; 'Pen' is also a female swan, so 'Pen chant' is a swan's song.
explanation.definitionFit: A farewell performance or last work is named after the swan's fabled dying song.

clue.text: Where Murphy's concerned it's no larceny

definitions.text: Where Murphy's concerned it's no larceny

parts.words: Where Murphy's concerned it's no larceny
parts.note: a murphy is slang for a potato, and digging potatoes is called this, the same word as slang for ...

explanation.surface: Someone called Murphy is cleared of theft.
explanation.walkthrough: Murphy is the Irish slang for a potato; harvesting potatoes uses the same word as slang for stealing, but taking spuds out of the ground is no crime.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means stealing as slang, and also digging up root crops at harvest.

clue.text: An upright lad one found in America or Spain

indicators.note: in a down clue a word standing upright reads from the bottom, so the word lad goes backwards

parts.note: taken as written, then turned

indicators.note: the figure for one is located inside the country's abbreviation

parts.note: USA, the United States of America
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: An honest young man is discovered in the New World or in Iberia.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'upright' means read from the bottom, so the lad is turned; 'found in' puts one inside the country. 'Spain' is a loose definition: the answer is a southern region of that country.
explanation.definitionFit: The region around Seville and Granada is part of the Iberian kingdom, so it stands here for the country.

clue.text: As one does the Romans in Rome

definitions.text: As one does the Romans in Rome

parts.words: As one does the Romans in Rome
parts.note: the proverb 'when in Rome, do as the Romans do' tells a visitor to copy local behaviour

explanation.surface: A remark about how a visitor behaves among the locals in Italy.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue leans on the proverb 'When in Rome, do as the Romans do': the visitor copies them.
explanation.definitionFit: Doing as the Romans do means copying their ways, which is mimicry.

clue.text: Where ladies have, issues for discussion?

definitions.text: Where ladies have, issues for discussion

parts.words: Where ladies have, issues for discussion
parts.note: 'issues' means offspring, so women with children gather to talk about them at a parish gathering

explanation.surface: A meeting where women debate agenda items.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Issues' looks like agenda items; it means children, so the ladies are parents at a club for parents.
explanation.definitionFit: A weekly church gathering for women with families, also a phrase for any cosy, chattering assembly.

definitions.note: the clue gives a plural; the answer is one such animal

indicators.note: something strange is out of its normal order, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: The first instalment of a series called Strange Beasts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Strange' rearranges PART I. The definition is plural and the answer singular, a liberty in this old puzzle.
explanation.definitionFit: The snouted hoofed mammal of the South American and Malayan forests is an odd-looking animal.

parts.note: Joseph Conrad wrote a novella about a ship caught in a tropical storm, and that storm is a huge wind

explanation.surface: A serious setback for a man named Conrad.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A big blow' sounds like a misfortune; it is a violent wind, and Typhoon is the title of Joseph Conrad's 1902 sea story.
explanation.definitionFit: A tropical cyclone in the western Pacific is a giant storm, and the title of Conrad's tale.

parts.note: Sal is a short form of the girl's name Sally
Ted is a short form of the boy's name Edward

explanation.surface: A parent remarking that a girl and boy are just like their own children.
explanation.walkthrough: A 'salted' mine has had ore planted in it to fool buyers; 'mine' looks like a possessive, not a pit.
explanation.definitionFit: A fraudster seeds a worthless claim with ore to make it look rich, which is called seasoning it in miners' slang.

clue.text: Too much of what you fancy spoils the child

definitions.text: Too much of what you fancy
definitions.meaning: excess in eating or pleasure, from the saying 'a little of what you fancy does you good'
giving a child everything it wants is what spoils it

explanation.definitionFit: Excess indulgence covers both gluttony and pampering a child until it is spoilt.

clue.text: The paper that provides the proof

definitions.text: The paper that provides the proof

parts.words: The paper that provides the proof
parts.note: a sworn written statement, signed before a notary, offered as evidence in court

explanation.surface: A document that settles an argument by proving the point.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Paper' and 'proof' suggest a newspaper or a printer's proof; the paper meant is a legal document sworn on oath.
explanation.definitionFit: A sworn written statement serves as evidence in legal proceedings.

definitions.meaning: a student taught by a teacher
the dark opening in the eye through which one sees

explanation.definitionFit: A school student is one sense; the other is the eye's aperture, which literally does the seeing.

clue.text: A tranquillizer for Bob the director of course

annotationWithheld.why: A tranquillizer for Bob the director of course (7): 'A tranquillizer' gives STILLER, but no source identifies the Bob Stiller who was a 'director of course', so the second definition cannot be explained honestly
annotationWithheld.clue: A tranquillizer for Bob the director of course

parts.note: the way in for noise: the opening of the ear canal

explanation.surface: A solid, reliable entry in a ledger or competition.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sound' reads as an adjective meaning reliable; it is the noun, and the entry is where it goes in.
explanation.definitionFit: The opening of the ear is the passage through which noise enters the head.

clue.text: Colonel, though drunk, gets top job in Abyssinia

definitions.meaning: a hot drink of port or sherry, sugar and spice; 'drunk' means he is a beverage
the title of the Ethiopian emperor

explanation.surface: An inebriated army officer is promoted to rule Ethiopia.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Though drunk' looks like an anagram signal or a slur on the colonel; it means the colonel's name is something that is drunk.
explanation.definitionFit: The spiced wine drink bears the surname of the colonel who devised it, and the same word was the Ethiopian monarch's title.

parts.note: a young chick still covered in soft fluff, not yet out of its nest

explanation.surface: A knowing, shrewd sort of person.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Downy' was slang for shrewd, so 'a downy bird' reads as a sharp customer; here it is a chick still in its first fluff.
explanation.definitionFit: A chick too young to leave home is still covered in fluffy down.

parts.note: 'tropically' means using tropes, figures of speech; Hamlet's 'words, words, words' are taken word for word

explanation.surface: A remark that the Danish prince was not in the tropics.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tropically' suggests hot climates; it means figuratively, using tropes. The opposite is word for word, and Hamlet answers 'Words, words, words'.
explanation.definitionFit: Taken word for word, with no figure of speech, is the opposite of figuratively.

clue.text: Its press is bad but it won't give up

indicators.note: a bad version of the words is a jumbled one, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A firm gets poor coverage in the newspapers but carries on regardless.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bad' rearranges ITS PRESS; 'is' and 'but it' link, the 'it' supplying the subject for the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To keep going in spite of opposition is to refuse to quit.

clue.text: Take back hard words to remove misconception ?

parts.note: the prefix dis- undoes or reverses what follows
abuse is harsh, insulting language

explanation.surface: Withdrawing harsh language to clear up a misunderstanding.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads as an apology; split the answer and it is the undoing prefix plus a word for insults.
explanation.definitionFit: To set someone right is to free them from a false belief.

parts.note: in algebra the small raised numbers that show what power a quantity is raised to

explanation.surface: Emblems of authority, like crowns and sceptres.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Symbols of power' suggests regalia; in mathematics the power is an exponent, written as a small raised figure.
explanation.definitionFit: Exponents are the raised figures that show how many times a number multiplies itself.

clue.text: Where 9 calls for loosening of a belt

definitions.text: Where 9 calls for loosening of a belt

parts.words: Where 9 calls for loosening of a belt
parts.note: 9 down is eating and drinking too much, which happens at the dining place and makes the waistband tight

explanation.surface: Somewhere excess makes a diner let out a notch.
explanation.walkthrough: The 9 is 9 down, OVERINDULGENCE; the place where you overeat is where you sit for meals.
explanation.definitionFit: Meals are eaten at this piece of furniture, where too much food is the usual reason to ease the belt.

clue.text: Country by way of being under the boil perhaps

indicators.note: in a down clue the second piece sits below the first
perhaps flags that the letters of boil are one possible arrangement, to be shuffled

parts.note: via means by way of

explanation.surface: Someone getting angry, as if a pot is about to boil over.
explanation.walkthrough: 'perhaps' rearranges BOIL to BOLI, and 'under' sets VIA below it in this down clue; 'being under the boil' reads as simmering with anger.
explanation.definitionFit: The landlocked South American republic is a nation.

definitions.meaning: a golf club with a large head, used for long tee shots

explanation.definitionFit: The longest-hitting golf club, formerly made of wood, shares its name with someone at the wheel of a car.

parts.note: a socialist anthem whose title is also a warning signal flown or waved to mark hazard

explanation.surface: A tune that warns people of peril.
explanation.walkthrough: The Red Flag is the British Labour Party's anthem; a red flag also signals danger, as on a firing range.
explanation.definitionFit: The anthem's title names the scarlet banner used as a hazard warning.

clue.text: How to catch a moke — look out !

indicators.note: the word look sits outside, around the animal, so the two letters of the word for look go round it

parts.note: lo is an old word meaning look
moke is slang for a donkey, an ass

explanation.surface: A warning cry about how to rope a donkey.
explanation.walkthrough: A moke is British slang for a donkey. 'out' wraps the old word for 'look' around the animal; 'a' links, and the definition hides behind the surface's cry of warning.
explanation.definitionFit: A cowboy's noosed rope is the way to catch stray animals.

parts.note: turtle doves are one kind; snapping reptiles of the same name are the other

explanation.surface: Even peaceful birds can lose their temper.
explanation.walkthrough: One word covers both the turtle dove and the snapping turtle, a shelled reptile that bites.
explanation.definitionFit: The name applies to a species of dove and to shelled reptiles known for snapping jaws.

definitions.meaning: clamps on a workbench that grip work in their jaws
two of the seven deadly sins, so examples of wickedness

explanation.definitionFit: Bench clamps share their name with moral failings, of which pride and gluttony are classic examples.

parts.note: a cat is said to have this many chances at living, and the cat-o'-nine-tails whip has nine tails

explanation.surface: Counting the lashes of a cat-o'-nine-tails.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'feline' with nine tails is the cat-o'-nine-tails whip; give each tail a life and you have the cat's proverbial allowance.
explanation.definitionFit: Cats proverbially survive eight brushes with death, getting nine existences in all.

definitions.meaning: returned to its former place or condition
..., that is put into storage again

explanation.definitionFit: Something brought back to its old state has been reinstated, and split after 're' it means put away in store again.

parts.note: rules made by a local authority, and split in two the words also say 'by means of statutes', which is how any government rules

explanation.surface: How authorities rule, at more than just council level.
explanation.walkthrough: Local councils pass these regulations, but split into two words they describe governing by legislation, which is not only local.
explanation.definitionFit: Local authorities and companies make rules of this kind, and any state governs through legislation.
